lessons.title: Meet matter’s building blocks
lessons.subtitle: Protons, neutrons and electrons
lessons.objective: Describe the charges and locations of the main subatomic particles.
paragraphs: An atom is a basic unit of an element. Its tiny nucleus contains protons and, in most atoms, neutrons. Protons carry positive charge, neutrons have no electric charge and electrons carry negative charge. The electron’s charge has the same magnitude as the proton’s charge, but the opposite sign.

The nucleus contains almost all of an atom’s mass. Electrons occupy the region around it. An electron is much less massive than a proton. A simple drawing of rings can help us count electrons, but it should not be mistaken for a photograph of fixed planetary paths.

In a neutral atom, the numbers of protons and electrons are equal, so their charges balance. Neutral does not mean that the atom contains no charged particles. Ordinary chemical changes mainly involve electrons; they do not usually change the number of protons in the nucleus.
lessons.example: A neutral carbon atom has 6 protons and 6 electrons. The charges balance even though the particles themselves are charged.
lessons.simple: Atom ke nucleus mein protons aur aam tor par neutrons hotay hain. Electrons nucleus ke gird region mein hotay hain. Neutral atom mein protons aur electrons ki tadaad barabar hoti hai.
takeaways: Protons are positive; electrons are negative.
The nucleus contains almost all the atomic mass.
Neutral atoms have equal proton and electron counts.
lessons.check: Why does a neutral atom still contain charged particles?

lessons.title: Read an atom’s identity card
lessons.subtitle: Atomic number and mass number
lessons.objective: Use atomic number and mass number to calculate proton and neutron counts.
paragraphs: The atomic number, Z, is the number of protons in an atom’s nucleus. It identifies the element. Every carbon atom has 6 protons. If the proton number changes, the element changes. Gaining or losing an electron does not change the element’s identity.

The mass number, A, counts protons plus neutrons in one nucleus. Therefore neutron number = A − Z. For carbon-14, A = 14 and Z = 6, so its nucleus contains 8 neutrons. A neutral carbon-14 atom has 6 electrons.

Mass number is a whole-number count for a particular isotope. It is different from the relative atomic mass shown for an element on many periodic tables, which reflects isotope masses and their abundances. Do not add the number of electrons to A.
lessons.example: A sodium-23 atom has Z = 11. It contains 11 protons and 23 − 11 = 12 neutrons. If it is neutral, it also has 11 electrons.
lessons.simple: Z protons ki tadaad hai. A protons aur neutrons ka total hai. Neutrons nikalnay ke liye A mein se Z minus karo.
takeaways: Atomic number Z equals the proton count.
Mass number A equals protons plus neutrons.
lessons.check: An atom has A = 27 and Z = 13. How many neutrons does it have?

lessons.title: Same element, different mass
lessons.subtitle: Isotopes and weighted averages
lessons.objective: Distinguish isotopes and calculate a simple isotope-weighted average.
paragraphs: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different neutron numbers. They have the same atomic number and different mass numbers. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons, but their neutron counts are 6 and 8. They are both carbon.

Isotopes have very similar chemical behaviour in many common situations because electron arrangement mainly controls chemical reactions. They can differ in mass and nuclear stability. Some isotopes are radioactive; not all isotopes are radioactive. Chemical isotope effects can occur, so “always identical” is too strong.

An element’s average atomic mass is weighted by isotope abundance. For an imaginary sample with equal numbers of isotopes of masses 10 u and 12 u, the average is 11 u. If the proportions are unequal, multiply each mass by its fractional abundance and add the products. The average does not mean every atom has that mass.
lessons.example: An imaginary mixture with 75% atoms of mass 10 u and 25% of mass 12 u has mean mass (0.75 × 10) + (0.25 × 12) = 10.5 u. This is an invented arithmetic example, not a claim about a real element.
lessons.simple: Isotopes aik hi element ke atoms hain: protons same, neutrons different. Average mass har isotope ki quantity ko dekh kar weighted average se nikalti hai.
takeaways: Isotopes share a proton number but differ in neutron number.
Average atomic mass is an abundance-weighted value.
lessons.check: Why can an element’s average atomic mass be a non-whole number?

lessons.title: When atoms gain or lose electrons
lessons.subtitle: Ions and electric charge
lessons.objective: Determine ionic charge from proton and electron counts.
paragraphs: An ion is an atom or a group of atoms with a net electric charge. A monatomic cation forms when an atom loses electrons. Losing negative charge makes its net charge positive. A monatomic anion forms when an atom gains electrons, producing a net negative charge.

For a single atom, charge in units of the elementary charge equals proton count minus electron count. A particle with 11 protons and 10 electrons has charge +1. Its nucleus still identifies it as sodium. A chloride ion with 17 protons and 18 electrons has charge −1.

Ion formation by ordinary electron transfer changes electron count, not proton count. A 2+ ion has two fewer electrons than its neutral atom. The “2+” does not mean two extra protons were added. Ions can also contain several bonded atoms, but the same idea of net charge applies.
lessons.example: Magnesium has 12 protons. Mg²⁺ has lost two electrons from the neutral atom, leaving 10 electrons. The proton number remains 12.
lessons.simple: Electron lose honay se positive ion banta hai; electron gain honay se negative ion. Charge = protons minus electrons. Element ki pehchan proton count se rehti hai.
takeaways: Losing electrons produces a positive ion.
Gaining electrons produces a negative ion.
Ionic charge does not by itself change proton number.
lessons.check: How many electrons are in a 2+ ion with 20 protons?

written.prompt: Distinguish atomic number from mass number.
written.answer: Atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus. Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in a particular nucleus.

written.prompt: What are isotopes? Give a clear example.
written.answer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different neutron numbers. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 each have 6 protons, but have 6 and 8 neutrons respectively.
keyPoints: Different neutron numbers with an example

written.prompt: Explain positive and negative ion formation, using sodium and chloride as examples.
written.answer: A neutral atom has equal proton and electron counts. When a sodium atom loses one electron, its 11 protons exceed its 10 remaining electrons by one, giving Na⁺. When a chlorine atom gains one electron, it has 17 protons and 18 electrons, giving Cl⁻. These changes involve electrons; the proton numbers and element identities remain unchanged.
